title: ICE Officer Indicted in Houston Had Been on Job Just Over a Year
excerpt: Mario Alberto Morales, a 2025 surge hire, surrendered Monday on an aggravated-assault indictment over an October 10 vehicle strike in Houston. He denies wrongdoing, ICE calls the case a political stunt — and his hiring record is now part of the story.
body:
• A Harris County grand jury has indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales, 33, on a second-degree felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon — the vehicle he was driving — over an October 10 incident in Houston that left Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, with multiple leg fractures.
  • Morales surrendered on Monday, was released on a $30,000 bond, and is next due in court on December 2, his attorney said. An indictment is an allegation, not a conviction: Morales is presumed innocent, his attorney calls the incident an accident, and ICE calls the case a political stunt.
  • Morales joined ICE in August 2025 as part of the administration's hiring surge and had been an Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little over a year — a record now at the center of scrutiny over how quickly the surge hires were vetted and trained.
  • District Attorney Sean Teare said his office has received no training records for Morales and questioned his prior work history; ICE and the officer's attorney dispute the prosecution's account and its motives.

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who had been on the job for a little over a year surrendered in a Houston courtroom on Monday after a Harris County grand jury indicted him in connection with running over a man who was on foot — a case that has put the Trump administration's rapid ICE hiring surge under scrutiny, NBC News reported. Mario Alberto Morales, 33, was released on a $30,000 bond after a hearing before District Court Judge Matthew Peneguy in Harris County, Texas, and his next court hearing is set for December 2, according to his attorney, David Lindenmuth, CNN reported.

The charge, and the incident behind it

A grand jury indicted Morales on Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, a second-degree felony, after he allegedly struck Miguel Parra Hernandez with an ICE vehicle near Houston on October 10, causing multiple leg fractures. The indictment, obtained by CNN, alleges Morales "intentionally, knowingly, and recklessly" caused serious bodily injury to Parra Hernandez "by striking the Complainant with a motor vehicle." Parra Hernandez, 48, is a Mexican national who has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years, has no criminal record and had no deportation order at the time, District Attorney Sean Teare said. He remains in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility; his attorney, Kim Bruno, said he suffered fractures and nerve damage and faces chronic pain. These are allegations in an indictment, not findings of fact: Morales has not been convicted of anything, and he is presumed innocent unless prosecutors prove the charge.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DfOMWarFwbL/

"The evidence that we have in this case is as clear as any I've ever prosecuted or investigated."

— Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, via CNN

Two accounts of October 10

Teare said video — the officer's body camera footage synced with surveillance video — showed Morales aggressively steering his vehicle into Parra Hernandez as the man fled on foot, and that Morales then called 911 to report that Parra Hernandez had "hit his car." ICE gives a different account: the agency said Parra Hernandez "ran in front of an ICE vehicle," said it "immediately contacted EMS and provided aid," and called the allegation that Morales struck him intentionally "RECKLESS and FALSE" in a statement to the Associated Press. Lindenmuth said the incident was an "accident," that his client did not commit a crime, and that the case amounts to "political prosecution" and "character assassination." ICE has also argued that local officials are not authorized to investigate federal officers following their duties. There is a further dispute about the operation itself: ICE said the target was a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, but Teare said the man by that name has been "apparently dead for nine years," and Parra Hernandez's brother said the person ICE was looking for was not the man riding with his brother.

https://x.com/CBSEveningNews/status/2117405935425507686

Why the officer's hiring is now part of the story

Morales was one of ICE's "surge hires" in August 2025, and had worked as an Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth told the Associated Press. Teare said his office has not received any training records for Morales, and questioned his background: "I can unequivocally tell you that I've reviewed thousands of job applications and resumes for law enforcement officers from around this state, and I'm not familiar with a single agency that would have hired this person, based on his past." NBC News reported that Morales previously worked several stints as a guard, including at the Port Isabel Detention Center, and that last year several Department of Homeland Security officials told NBC News some ICE recruits had failed to meet the standards for hire, including having disqualifying criminal backgrounds or lacking physical or academic requirements; DHS told NBC News at the time that most of its new recruits are former law enforcement officers. Earlier this month, the agency said it would retrain thousands of officers who had received expedited training due to the hiring surge, NBC News reported, and CNN reported that the surge cut in half the amount of time new agents are trained before they are deployed. Morales's attorney said his client had more training than other hires.

What happens next

Morales is due back in court on December 2. NBC News reported he is the first ICE agent indicted in Texas, and the Associated Press noted he is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. Teare's office is separately investigating a fatal shooting by an ICE officer in Houston this summer. The case is now two stories at once: a criminal prosecution that will turn on video the jury can see for itself, and a public argument about how fast ICE grew, and what that speed cost in vetting and training.
nri_angle: The case tests how the rapid expansion of ICE's workforce is vetted and trained — a question with direct consequences for immigrant communities, including Indian nationals, facing enforcement.
author: Diaspora Desk

items.text: Officer Morales indicted on October 10 incident.
Victim Miguel Parra Hernandez suffered multiple leg fractures.
Next court hearing scheduled for December 2.
